correctness.rationale: The membership cells for the m variables partition the underlying atom set. Every feasible nonempty support is realized by assigning at least one atom to each type and the remaining atoms arbitrarily among those types. Operations preserve the property that the output is a union of cells determined solely by the support: the endpoint test checks only whether the chosen subset of types is empty or the whole support. Conversely the term δ₀(Y)=¬Y∧circ(Y) detects emptiness, so testing each cell defines exact-support selectors that realize any choice of output union on each feasible support. Constants for empty joins/meets are definable since m≥1. Independent choices of 2^r outputs at each r-element support give the displayed count and examples. The same inductively defined type semantics on every allowed support proves inclusion of the at-most-m-variable identity theories as k increases; exact support tests of size k+1 separate successive theories while k<2^m, and beyond that no new support can appear. This proves the ideal boundary statements even for k=1 and m=1. Independent concrete term-table closure on full input/atom coordinates (not assuming support collapse) used the additivity of ∃X, which tests nonemptiness, to refine Boolean blocks; it verified the exponents 4,16,28,32,32 for m=2 and k=1..5 among other cases. evidence: Halmos's simple/semisimple/functional representation supplies the classical monadic framework. Baker–Pixley in the cited text says that on a finite algebra with a majority term, preservation of subalgebras of the square suffices for term representability. Here a majority term follows from the definable equality switch.
broader_coverage.reasoning: In the Boolean reduct a subalgebra of the square corresponds to a partition of two disjoint copies of [k]. If any block is supported on only one side, its image under ∃ is the whole of that side and zero on the other; thus the whole side is a union of blocks, forcing the subalgebra to be a product. Otherwise every block meets both sides, so the subalgebra is the graph of the isomorphism of the two projection subalgebras that matches their blocks. This is why preserving generated subalgebras and their isomorphisms is sufficient here; the discriminator does not assert unrestricted arbitrary tables on B_k.

evidence: A tuple generates precisely the Boolean algebra of unions of its occupied cells; ∃ produces only Boolean constants so adds nothing to this subalgebra. Two such generated subalgebras admit an isomorphism carrying generators to generators exactly when the supports coincide, in which case it must carry each cell to its equally labelled cell.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: In particular an arbitrary support-wise choice preserves all product and graph subalgebras of the square, so Lemma 10.4 gives it as a term. Necessity follows from preservation, too. The resulting term algebra is the product of the simple powersets on feasible supports, one factor per nonempty P with |P|≤k. Its size and sharp cutoff are immediate. Projections onto fewer factors give the restriction maps; the selector of any newly allowed factor separates identities. This is a direct routine specialization, not a claim that Halmos's inspected passages display the formula verbatim.
